facts.statement: The study asked if biological sex, puberty timing, and childhood mental health symptoms could predict how visual attention brain waves change from childhood to adulthood.
facts.subject: humans

facts.statement: Researchers used a longitudinal cohort design with 531 youth who performed a reaction-time task at five specific ages between 2010 and 2025.
facts.subject: humans

facts.statement: The main finding was that the visual P300 brain wave showed a curved decline pattern from late childhood into early adulthood.
facts.subject: humans

facts.statement: Boys with higher levels of externalizing behaviors or depression symptoms at age 9 started with lower baseline visual P300 brain waves.
facts.subject: humans

facts.statement: The authors note that further research is needed to understand how these neural attention markers develop and connect to future mental health issues.
facts.subject: humans
